kept.spine: The defensive arrangements at Hochhausen are thin, standing up to ordinary pressure and giving out against anything sustained.
A stranger wronged here finds there is nowhere to take it, and nobody here expected there to be.
faces: A traveller says a stranger who is wronged here has nowhere to take it but the door of whoever did it.
A woman at the long table says a stranger owed money here is paid in goods and told not to wait on coin.
One of the elders says a stranger's complaint is heard the same as anyone's, and one who does not stay to hear the answer was not wronged much.
A local priest holds that the ground takes a stranger on the same terms as anyone else here, whatever was agreed or not agreed beforehand.
At the gate they say a stranger is looked over on the way in, and nothing is kept of the looking.
The muster tells a stranger who complains that there is nowhere to lock up the man he names. There is nowhere for the stranger either.
The stallholders say a stranger who is cheated here has no board to complain to, and does best to come back to the stall himself.

kept.spine: Everyone here has seen who turns out when something is needed, and takes it that the same few would turn out for anything worse.
faces: A traveller says what is handed over here is goods, not coin, and nothing more comes with it.
The older heads here say a request is made out loud, in front of the neighbours, and a refusal is heard by the same ears that heard the asking.
The potboy says the loudest at the table is always the household asked last, and the ones asked first sit quietly over their cups.
A local priest says a household gives toward a burial whatever it has, and what is given is remembered by the neighbours better than any count kept of it.
Those who hold the way through say the bar coming down is heard at the far doors. Not one of the doors opens.
The muster reckons what comes up from a door is a body or a tool, and the tool is remembered as well as the body.
At the market they say the town draws from whoever can be found, and nothing is easier to find than a stall.
One of the watch says the same corners get stood in whether the purse is settled or not. The round ends where it starts, at the water.
Nobody here asks the soldiers their business, the soldiers say, and everybody here asks them for a hand.

kept.poolKey: Disasters & Famine: NO reserves, NO medical provision
kept.spine: A stranger who asks here for a grain store is shown a field, and one who asks for a house for the sick is shown an ordinary door.
faces: A carter reckons the sacks that leave a house for the mill are counted going out and never counted coming back.
A woman at the long table says a stranger who asks for a house for the sick is taken to be sick himself, and served right there at the door.
The older heads here hold that what a stranger calls a lack is only how the place has always been arranged, and they do not say who arranged it.
The people who keep the register say part of the ground digs easily and part does not, and everyone here already knows which is which.
At the market they say a buyer can get grain on a market day and nowhere at all to store it afterward.

kept.spine: Enforcement and criminal presence at Hochhausen sit close enough that which way the next few seasons go is still an open question.

kept.poolKey: First-Survey qualification (the reading is a first look)
kept.spine: The safety reading for Hochhausen is an initial one. It says plainly what has been seen so far and nothing about what has not.
A stranger asking after the arrangements at Hochhausen is met with genuine incomprehension, and there is no telling whether that is the truth or a very good performance of it.
The town has no boundary at Hochhausen, only an edge that sits wherever the last building happens to stand.
A stranger at Hochhausen finds a hall whose business is the kind of trouble a garrison is the wrong tool for, and finds it a busy place.
Nothing here answers a threat it cannot see, and that is exactly where the town stands exposed.
No wall marks where Hochhausen ends, and at this size the country and the town simply agree to differ.
The town eats what arrives and keeps nothing put by for a season when nothing does.
